name: Protein timing

card.summary: Spreading protein across the day and around workouts or before sleep to support muscle growth and recovery, and with it a more muscular physique.
card.aka: Nutrient timing, anabolic window, pre-sleep protein
card.note: Researchers generally report that total daily protein intake explains most of the effect; timing adds smaller differences.

quick.overview:
Protein timing is the practice of planning when protein is eaten relative to training and sleep, for example a serving after a workout, protein spread over several meals, or a casein-type serving before bed. Lifters use it to support muscle growth and recovery, which shows up as a fuller, more muscular physique.

Meta-analyses of resistance-training trials report that protein supplementation after exercise and at night was associated with small gains in muscle or strength compared with placebo, while analyses that compare different timings directly have found little or no difference. Total daily intake is usually described as the larger factor.
quick.how: Common patterns are a protein-containing meal or shake around the workout, three to five protein-containing meals across the day, and a slow-digesting protein before sleep. People combine this with resistance training and calorie targets suited to their goal.
quick.risks: Protein timing is a low-risk dietary habit for healthy people. Those with kidney disease or other medical conditions are generally advised by clinicians to ask about protein intake first, and supplements vary in quality.

lead: Protein timing, or nutrient timing, treats the timing of eating relative to exercise as part of muscle development, alongside total intake [1]. Its best-known idea is the anabolic window, a period of roughly 15 to 45 minutes after exercise when athletes often time carbohydrate and protein intake [1].

Lifters use it as a way to support the muscle growth behind a larger, more defined physique. Typical patterns include protein after training, protein spread evenly over meals and a serving before sleep [2][3]. Reviews describe a muscle-building intake of about 1.6 g per kilogram of body weight per day, spread over four meals or snacks, as sufficient in one 2018 review [2].

Meta-analyses of randomised trials give a mixed picture on timing itself. A network meta-analysis of 116 trials with 4,711 participants found protein after exercise and at night were the most effective timings for muscle mass and strength respectively compared with placebo [3], while a 2025 meta-analysis of studies directly comparing intake before and after exercise found no effect of timing on chest press strength [4].

angle.text: Lifters schedule protein to support recovery and growth, which accumulates into more muscle. Researchers describe total daily protein as the main driver, with timing adding smaller differences.

paras: Nutrient timing rests on two factors: the proportions of nutrients consumed and their timing relative to exercise [1]. After resistance training, muscle protein synthesis stays elevated for a period; one study found it returned to baseline around 28 hours after training in young men, and another found it still elevated at 72 hours [2].
Cumulative muscle protein synthesis, the total synthesis summed across a day, has been proposed as a way to study how total intake and timing interact in free-living conditions [5].

In gyms and forums the practice usually takes three forms. The first is protein soon after training, often as a shake. The second is distributing protein across several meals; one small study found that a 90 g protein meal raised muscle protein synthesis no more than a 30 g meal, though that study did not include training and its conclusions are disputed [2]. The third is pre-sleep protein, usually a slow-digesting casein product [3].

A 2013 meta-analysis in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition examined protein timing and muscle strength and hypertrophy [6]. A review in the same journal in 2012 stated that two tenets matter most for weight trainers: 1.2 to 2.0 g of protein per kilogram of body weight and sufficient calories, and it examined whether timing of protein supplements adds to that [7].

In the 2024 network meta-analysis of resistance-training trials, post-exercise protein produced a mean difference of 0.54 kg in fat-free mass and 0.34 kg in skeletal muscle mass compared with placebo, and night-time protein showed the largest strength differences, with moderate certainty; no timing or type improved physical performance [3]. A 2025 meta-analysis limited to head-to-head comparisons of before versus after exercise found no timing effect for chest press repetition maximum [4].

A randomised trial in postmenopausal women reported that protein timing had no effect on lean mass, strength or functional capacity gains [8]. A trial in professional cyclists examined pre-sleep protein while accounting for timing versus total protein [9].

Randomised trials and meta-analyses have compared post-exercise, pre-exercise and pre-sleep protein for lean mass and strength. The 2024 network meta-analysis included 116 trials and 4,711 participants and found modest benefits for post-exercise and night-time supplementation compared with placebo [3]. The 2025 meta-analysis of direct before-versus-after comparisons found no difference for chest press strength [4]. A trial in postmenopausal women found no effect of timing [8].
